sections.body_en:
Out of awe and fear in the face of the gravity of the subject and the memory of the holy ones who were killed for kiddush Hashem, and out of love for every person created in the image of God, and respect for all who believe in God and pray for repentance and redemption, I will try to explain the Torah's position regarding the Christian religion. At the outset I will preface that there is no pretension here to encompass the Christian religion in all its branches, but rather to focus on Judaism's general position regarding Christianity.

The Christian religion caused the people of Israel great pain and terrible suffering. As a result of our sins, foremost among them the sin of baseless hatred, the Romans conquered the Land of Israel. Many in Israel were drawn after foreign ideas, the various groups fought one another, and it seemed that unless a tremendous movement of repentance took place in Israel, the Second Temple would be destroyed and Israel would go into exile, and all the curses written in the Torah for breaking the covenant with God were about to befall Israel. True, Sages and righteous men arose in Israel who continued to pave the way of Torah and established a Torah foundation that later turned out to be what sustained the people throughout the long exile; but they did not succeed in magnifying Torah in such a way that the entire people would unite around the values of Torah and mitzvot. To many it seemed at that time that the people of Israel had reached the end of its road, that the great vision of bringing blessing to all the families of the earth would no longer be fulfilled; instead, trouble upon trouble descended upon Israel, and the curses written in the Torah began to be fulfilled.

Out of this despair the Christian religion was founded and took shape. It claimed that the people of Israel had failed in its destiny to realise the word of God and bring about the repair of the world, and therefore God's choice of Israel had been annulled, and the value of the Torah's mitzvot had been annulled as well. From then on, the redemption written in the Torah would come through a "New Covenant" by means of "that man," who is "God" who appeared in the world in the form of flesh and blood. The Christian religion turned to all human beings equally and claimed that from now on its believers are the true Israel, while the Jews are "Israel of the flesh," who will be saved only if they convert to Christianity. And the Jews who did not convert bear responsibility for the death of "that man," and responsibility for postponing the redemption of the world and for all the suffering caused as a result; therefore there is no end to their punishment in this world and in the World to Come.

Against this position, which came to uproot the foundations of Israel's faith, its value as a nation and the obligation to keep the mitzvot, Israel stood firm for their lives, and did not agree to regard the Christians as a Jewish stream, but rather as minim, that is, seemingly similar but in truth different in essence.1

notes_en.en: Berakhot 28b: "Rabban Gamliel said to the Sages: Is there anyone who knows how to compose the blessing against the minim? Shmuel Ha-katan stood up and composed it." Rav Kook explained in Ein Aya there that since this is a blessing containing hatred for the enemies of Israel, in order that the hatred not become second nature and spread beyond what necessity requires, it had to be composed by Shmuel Ha-katan, who was careful to remove the feeling of hatred from his heart even toward his mortal enemies, as he was accustomed to say (Avot 4:19): "When your enemy falls, do not rejoice, and when he stumbles, let your heart not be glad, lest the Lord see it and it be displeasing in His eyes, and He turn His anger away from him" (Mishlei 24:17). Of him it was said that he was humble and pious (Sanhedrin 11a). See Peninei Halakha, Tefilla 17:10, note 7. On the definition of minim, see above 5, note 13.

sections.title_en: The Saga of Suffering and Bloodshed
sections.body_en:
After about three hundred years, Christianity became the ruling religion in most of the lands where Jews lived, and then, in the name of Christianity, priests and rulers oppressed and humiliated Jews, plundered their property, expelled them from their places and inherited their homes, and not infrequently even murdered them. True, in general the official position of the Church was that the Jews should be oppressed in order thereby to prove the truth of Christianity, which had inherited [the place of] Israel, but that they should not be murdered or harmed excessively. However, since according to the Christian conception the Jews were guilty of the murder of "God" and of the evil in the world, a fierce hatred developed toward them. Over the generations, many attributed to them every bad trait. They defined them as greedy, lustful, cruel, cunning and xenophobic. They blamed them for all the troubles in the world, including poisoning wells, spreading diseases and murdering Christian children in order to use their blood for baking matzot for Pesaḥ. As a result, many times the position in practice was more terrible than the official position: masses of people, encouraged by priests and monks, rioted against Jews, plundered their property and murdered them, and kings and rulers expelled them from their lands while dispossessing them of their property. Even the Nazis, who were secular, under the influence of that same legacy of hatred, carried out the most terrible murder in history, of six million Jews who were not at war with any nation or state.

Likewise, although the official position of the Church was not to force Jews to convert, in practice harsh decrees of confiscation of property and expulsion were often imposed on anyone who would not convert, and not infrequently Jews who refused to convert were even threatened with death. Many Jews withstood the test and preferred to sacrifice all their property on the altar of their faith, and in many cases even gave up their lives for kiddush Hashem; but there were also many who did not withstand the harsh test and converted. Over the long course of history, under threat of death or expulsion and confiscation of property, millions of Jews were forced to change their religion, to the point that some estimate that about ten percent of the peoples of Europe are descendants of Jews who were forced to change their religion. Even when the conversion was done under coercion, the Jews were forbidden to return to their religion, and the death penalty was even imposed on those who returned to Judaism. To enforce this law, for hundreds of years the Inquisition would interrogate converted Jews suspected of keeping Jewish mitzvot in secret. Under terrible torture the converts were forced to confess their "sin," and even to inform on their friends, who in turn were taken for interrogation by the Inquisition. After the "confession," the condemned were put to death by burning at the stake, beheading or hanging, according to the severity of the "sin." All this took place in a public ceremony called an auto-da-fé (act of faith), which Jews and converts were obliged to watch. The property of the murdered was confiscated, and their orphaned children, who were forced to watch their parents' execution, were left destitute to die in the street of hunger or disease, or to be taken to monasteries and educated as Christians.

The pages would run out and the saga of suffering that the Jews endured at the hands of the Christians over nearly two thousand years would not be finished: from the days of the rule of Rome and Byzantium, through the Crusades in Ashkenaz, the terrible pogroms of the year [5]151 (1391) against the great Jewish communities of Spain, the expulsion from Spain in the year [5]252 (1492), and all the persecutions, expulsions and pogroms that took place in all the lands of Europe, from west to east, under all the streams of Christianity: Catholic, Protestant and the Orthodox in the Slavic lands.

Even today, when by God's kindness the words of the prophets have begun to be fulfilled, and the people of Israel is returning to the Land of Israel, to build it and make its wastelands bloom, the blood of the murdered Jews cries out to us from the ground. The weeping of the millions of Jews who were humiliated and expelled destitute still echoes in our ears. The groan of the Jews who were forcibly converted to Christianity echoes in hidden places, and the silent weeping of tens of millions of their descendants living in Europe and America who do not know their origin pierces the void of the world. The Lord is a God of vengeance; may He avenge the vengeance of His children from the hand of those who shed their blood and tormented them. Despite all this, we have not abandoned our faith in the redemption of Israel, and we still cleave to our destiny to bring blessing to all the families of the earth, and we believe that the world can be repaired with righteousness and justice, with kindness and compassion, and our hearts are full of love for all human beings who desire good and abhor evil. In this spirit we will continue to explain this painful subject.

God chose the people of Israel to be His treasured people; He brought them out of Egypt, gave them the Torah and made an eternal covenant with them, to be the bearer of His word to the world and to bring blessing to all the peoples. God gave man and Israel the ability to choose between good and evil: if Israel choose to keep the covenant, they will merit great blessing, and if they break the covenant and abandon God, His Torah and His mitzvot, they will be punished with terrible severity, as explained at great length in the portions of Beḥukotai and Ki Tavo. However, this choice of Israel cannot annul the Divine covenant that God made with Israel, and cannot annul the Divine promise of the redemption of Israel and the world; it can only determine whether the process of repair and redemption will take place gently and swiftly, or through long and harsh suffering.

When Israel sinned to the point that they could no longer repair their situation without the atonement of exile and suffering, all the harsh words of calamity in the Torah began to be fulfilled. As it is stated (Devarim 28:15-68): "But it shall come to pass, if you will not listen to the voice of the Lord your God, to observe to do all His commandments and His statutes which I command you this day, that all these curses shall come upon you and overtake you: Cursed shall you be in the city, and cursed shall you be in the field… Cursed shall you be when you come in, and cursed shall you be when you go out… The Lord shall cause you to be smitten before your enemies… and you shall be a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth… And your carcass shall be food for all the birds of the heavens and the beasts of the earth, and none shall frighten them away… And you shall become an astonishment, a proverb and a byword among all the peoples where the Lord shall lead you. And all these curses shall come upon you and pursue you and overtake you until you are destroyed, because you did not listen to the voice of the Lord your God, to keep His commandments and His statutes which He commanded you… Therefore you shall serve your enemies whom the Lord shall send against you, in hunger and in thirst, in nakedness and in want of all things, and He shall put a yoke of iron upon your neck until He has destroyed you." The words of the Torah about the nations were also fulfilled, that they would be shaken and ask: "Why has the Lord done thus to this land?! What is the heat of this great anger?! Then they shall say: Because they forsook the covenant of the Lord, the God of their fathers, which He made with them when He brought them out of the land of Egypt, and went and served other gods and bowed down to them… And the anger of the Lord was kindled against that land, to bring upon it all the curse that is written in this book. And the Lord uprooted them from their land in anger and in wrath and in great indignation, and cast them into another land, as at this day" (ibid. 29:23-27). The Christian religion interpreted the fulfilment of the curses as proof that God had decided to break His covenant with His people Israel. Therefore they called the Tanakh the "Old Testament" (literally, the Old Covenant), and the books about the founding of the Christian religion the "New Testament" (New Covenant), which replaced it.

But Israel withstood the terrible test and strengthened themselves in their faith in God's promise that He would never break His covenant with them, "For the Lord will not forsake His people, nor will He abandon His inheritance" (Tehillim 94:14). They believed that God loves them, and therefore He chastises and educates them, as explained in the Torah in the portions of the blessings and curses. As it is stated (Devarim 8:5): "As a man chastises his son, so the Lord your God chastises you." For only the people chosen to reveal to the world God's light and blessing does God chastise and refine, so that it may fulfil its destiny. As it is stated (Amos 3:2): "You only have I known of all the families of the earth; therefore I will visit upon you all your iniquities." Every morning and evening Israel would strengthen themselves in prayer and recite Keri'at Shema with its blessings, mentioning that God is the Creator of all, of darkness and light, and that even evil comes from Him and all is for the good. Thereby they were strengthened in the faith that God loves them with an eternal love, and they praised and thanked God for this: "Blessed are You, Lord, who chooses His people Israel in love." With awe and fear they accepted upon themselves the yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven: "Hear, O Israel, the Lord is our God, the Lord is one," and they accepted upon themselves to love God and to give up their lives for the sanctity of His Name: "And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might." "With all your soul – even if He takes your soul; and with all your might – with all your wealth" (Mishna Berakhot 9:5). In this spirit they remembered the Exodus from Egypt and believed that God would redeem them, and they praised and thanked God for this: "Blessed are You, Lord, who redeemed Israel."

Even when the suffering intensified greatly, and a terrible darkness covered the whole earth, Israel strengthened themselves in their faith that just as all the curses written in the Torah were fulfilled, so too all the prophecies of redemption in the Torah and the Prophets would be fulfilled, and God would return and redeem them. As it is stated after the curses in the portion of Beḥukotai (Vayikra 26:42-44): "Then I will remember My covenant with Yaakov, and also My covenant with Yitzḥak, and also My covenant with Avraham will I remember, and I will remember the land… And yet for all that, when they are in the land of their enemies, I will not reject them, nor will I abhor them, to destroy them utterly and to break My covenant with them, for I am the Lord their God." And likewise it is stated after the curses in the book of Devarim (29:3-5): "Then the Lord your God will return your captivity and have compassion on you, and will return and gather you from all the peoples where the Lord your God has scattered you. If your dispersed are at the ends of the heavens, from there the Lord your God will gather you and from there He will take you. And the Lord your God will bring you into the land which your fathers possessed, and you shall possess it, and He will do you good and multiply you above your fathers."

Christianity did indeed receive from Judaism the principle of belief in one God, but at the same time it claimed that "that man" is "God" who became incarnate in flesh and blood, and that the one Divinity is a Trinity – the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Many debates raged among Christians about the definition of all this, but in general it is agreed by almost all streams and sects that that man who appeared on earth as flesh and blood is in essence "God." As Rabbi Yehuda Ha-levi summarised the Christians' belief (Kuzari 1:4): "Human in the revealed and divine in the hidden, a prophet sent in the revealed and a God who sends prophets in the hidden; and he is the messiah, who is called the son of God, and he is the Father and he is the Son and he is the Holy Spirit."

This conception is called "idolatry in shituf," since in addition to faith in God they associate an idolatrous conception, according to which the one Divinity, which is beyond all definition, becomes embodied in a human being and in a Trinity. For Israel, "idolatry in shituf" is considered idolatry in every respect, and a Jew is obligated to give up his life rather than sin in this. If a Jew is presented with the option of accepting the Christian faith or being killed, he is obligated to be killed and not convert to Christianity (above 4:7). Apparently, that is why Jews are careful always to call the one in whom Christians believe "that man," in order to emphasise that he is a man and not God.

However, regarding Bnei Noaḥ, according to most poskim, "idolatry in shituf" was not forbidden (above 5:8-10). For as long as the moral and spiritual state of the world is not suited to faith in God's unity in its purity, there is a concern that if human beings do not believe at all, their moral state may be much worse. In support of this position, some cite as an example the Nazis in Germany and the Communists in Russia: two movements of wickedness and murderousness that grew among people who had abandoned faith in God through the Christian religion, and led to monstrous wickedness beyond anything that was customary in the periods when people believed in Christianity. Moreover, in the view of many of the great Sages of Israel, Christians who conduct themselves morally toward every person and toward Israel, despite the idolatrous aspect of shituf in their faith, can be considered pious and righteous, each person according to his level (above 5:13).

Similarly, our master Rav Kook, of blessed memory, wrote that although the idolatrous error is bad and harmful, its wickedness is grave only when it causes evil deeds. Therefore the main venom in Christianity, as also in Islam, is not in the idolatrous conception but in uprooting the value of the mitzvot and good deeds, and in the bad attitude toward the people of Israel and the hope of its redemption (Shemona Kevatzim 1:30-32).2

notes_en.en: In Orot, Yisrael U-teḥiyato 4, the nature of the spiritual venom in harming the unique quality (segula) of Israel and blurring national identities is explained: because of it, faith illuminates everything equally but only feebly, and does not illuminate fully each people and family as befits them, and all the shades of reality as is fitting for them. As a result, many become estranged from faith and act wickedly. Rav Eliyahu Benamozegh (5583-5660) of Italy, with his breadth of learning and depth of understanding, expanded and delved deeply into this subject, and his important words are brought in the book "Jewish Morality versus Christian Morality" in the translation of Rav Eliyahu Raḥamim Zini. His words, together with the words of our master Rav Kook, are the basis for the following three sections, including the critique of Christian morality together with recognition of its positive side. In his fundamental inquiry, Rav Benamozegh also proved that the positive foundations in Christianity, in which Christianity supposedly elevates itself above Judaism, were learned from the explicit words of the Sages of Israel who preceded them.

sections.body_en:
Since the Christians gave corporeal form to abstract faith in a human figure, they had something tangible to cleave to, and thus they could draw to their religion many people from various peoples who were accustomed to idol worship. However, this carries a moral price relative to Judaism in two main areas: 1) the loss of pure faith in God's unity; 2) the loss of personal responsibility for the repair of man and the world.

1) The loss of pure faith in God's unity: according to the Christian conception, which is tainted with idolatry, "God" is defined within a particular domain, and consequently everything outside it is utterly evil, and Satan rules it. In this conception, Satan has enormous power of dominion over this entire world, which is fundamentally corrupt, to the point that even "God" did not succeed in repairing it, and when he tried, evil overpowered him and killed him. Thus the world remains sunk in sin until the time comes when "God" will be able to overcome Satan.

But according to the truth, God created everything – the heavens and the earth, light and darkness, good and evil – and everything He created, He created for the good. In the first stage, thanks to evil, man was given the possibility of revealing the Divine image within him and choosing good. In the second stage, through the correct guidance of the Torah and the mitzvot, man can cleave to the ways of God and transform darkness and evil into good, and thereby the world is progressively redeemed.

2) The loss of man's personal responsibility for the repair of the world. For if even "God" cannot repair the world for the time being, all the more so it is impossible for human beings to repair it, since sin envelops the world and man. That is, the mitzvot and good deeds do not have the power to repair man and the world, which are sunk in sin. Rather, the salvation of human beings depends only on their believing in "that man," who is "God," and that through his suffering and death on earth he redeemed them from original sin. And they must ask forgiveness for being sunk in sin and confess their iniquity. All the value of good deeds is only for the refinement of a person's soul and the strengthening of his faith, but they do not have the power to repair the world itself.

By contrast, according to faith in God's unity, God created man in His image, endowed him with reason and conscience, and placed in his hands the responsibility for repairing the world, as it is stated (Tehillim 115:16): "The heavens are the heavens of the Lord, but the earth He has given to the children of men." Therefore God gave Israel the Torah and the mitzvot, so that through their understanding of the Torah and through their good deeds they would elevate all areas of life and reveal the Divine light in them. Thus, through countless beneficial studies and good deeds, of Israel and of all the righteous and pious among the nations of the world, the world will be elevated and the Divine blessing will rest upon it.

sections.title_en: The Value of the Mitzvot, Justice, Family and Property
sections.body_en:
Christianity claimed against Judaism that it is morally superior to it: instead of dealing with the small deeds of the mitzvot, it demands of a person faith, love and intention. But in truth, Christianity's position rests on despair of the world that God created, and on despair of man, created in the image of God, as one who cannot repair his life and the world through his good deeds. Whereas according to the faith of Israel, it is within a person's power to cleave to the Torah and the mitzvot, to overcome his evil inclinations and turn them to the good. And even if he sometimes stumbles, he has the possibility of repenting and continuing to repair.

As a result of despairing of repairing the world itself, Christianity claimed that there is no value in dealing with law and justice, since in any case all the matters of this world over which people quarrel are unimportant, and it is fitting for believers to act with kindness and forbearance. Therefore the Christian religion does not deal with the legal system, which it perceives as morally low. But in practice it is not possible always to act with kindness, for there is a limit to the abundance in the world, and there is no way to divide it without just law. And if there is no justice, then the wicked take over the world, and robbery and bloodshed multiply without end. In contrast to the Christian religion, which does not deal with law, Judaism deals extensively with the repair of law and society. According to the faith of Israel, dealing with law expresses faith in God's unity, according to which there is no domain that the Divine light does not illuminate and guide, and only thus are all of human life and the world sanctified (Yisrael U-teḥiyato 3).

Following on from this, a prevalent position in Christianity is that marriage is a necessary evil, because the bond between a man and his wife is steeped in sin, and whoever can is better off abstaining from marriage. But according to the Torah, it is a great mitzva to marry, and the Shekhina rests between spouses who live faithfully and love and gladden one another. For the Divine unity rests between them in miniature, since through marriage the spouses unite into one. The soul and the body too unite together in this mitzva, and the inclination of desire, which is liable to lead a person astray, is transformed through marriage into a mitzva. The lofty idea of faithfulness and unity joins with physical pleasure, and the moral value of total devotion joins with the greatest joy (Peninei Halakha, Simḥat Ha-bayit U-virkhato 1:1; 5).

The same applies to the attitude toward property and money. According to the prevalent position in Christianity, work intended to acquire property beyond what is necessary is reprehensible, as it expresses greed. Extensive dealing with money too – money-changing, banking and commerce – is perceived as low, negative and opposed to holiness, to the point that it is fitting to overturn tables and rise up against it. But according to faith in God's unity, property and abundance too express the Divine blessing, for God desires the good of His creatures in this world. Rather, the challenge is that together with rejoicing over all the good that God has given him, a person should use his property to add goodness and blessing to the world, and, as the Torah commands, support Torah scholars, help the poor and fulfil mitzvot. Therefore, when the Torah explains the blessing that will come to those who believe in God and keep the mitzvot, it describes material blessing. And therefore, when we pray for good, we do not pray for a meagre livelihood just sufficient to survive, but ask God for an ample livelihood, so that we can rejoice in the Divine abundance and bless God for the good He has bestowed upon us.

The attitude toward repentance too is completely different. According to Christianity, a person has no real possibility of repairing his sins, since in any case as long as he is in this world he is sunk in sin and evil, and his salvation depends on faith in "God" – "that man," who through his suffering redeemed all who cleave to him. Therefore forgiveness (forbearance) is an important foundation in Christianity. It is directed also to the wicked who have sinned greatly: since the evil inclination is so strong, their guilt is lesser, and if they submit and ask forgiveness, they will be forgiven. By contrast, according to the faith of Israel, the sinner is required to repent in a way that involves actual repair: it begins with a commitment to stop sinning, and continues with the sinner's effort to repair everything he spoiled, to appease the people he hurt, and to return what he stole. Thus, gradually, man and humanity progress toward the repair of the world.

Together with the enormous pain and terrible suffering that the Jewish people endured from the Christians, and together with the harsh claims against the Christian religion, it is fitting to look also at its positive side. The Christian religion spread in the world ideas of faith and morality whose foundation is in the Tanakh and the heritage of Israel. As Rambam wrote (Hilkhot Melakhim 11:4), "Jesus of Nazareth" was indeed not the messiah, for the messiah will gather the dispersed of Israel and strengthen them in keeping the mitzvot, whereas "this one caused Israel to be destroyed by the sword, their remnant to be scattered and humiliated, the Torah to be changed, and most of the world to err and serve a god besides the Lord. But the thoughts of the Creator of the world – no man has the power to grasp them, for our ways are not His ways and our thoughts are not His thoughts. And all these matters of Jesus of Nazareth, and of that Ishmaelite who arose after him, are only to pave the way for the King Messiah and to prepare the whole world to serve the Lord together, as it is stated: 'For then I will turn to the peoples a pure language, that they may all call upon the Name of the Lord, to serve Him with one consent' (Tzefania 3:9). How so? The whole world has already become filled with the words of the messiah, the words of the Torah and the words of the mitzvot, and these words have spread to distant islands and among many peoples of uncircumcised heart, and they discuss these matters and the mitzvot of the Torah. Some say: These mitzvot were true but have already lapsed in this time and were not in force for all generations. And others say: They contain hidden meanings and are not to be taken literally, and the messiah has already come and revealed their hidden meanings. But when the King Messiah truly arises and succeeds and is exalted and lifted up, they will all immediately return and know that their fathers inherited falsehood, and that their prophets and fathers led them astray." So wrote Rabbi Yehuda Ha-levi (Kuzari 4:23), and Ramban, who cited the words of Rambam and expanded on them (Derashat Torat Hashem Temima, Kitvei Ramban, vol. 1, pp. 143-144).

In addition to the fact that Christianity advanced humanity another stage toward redemption, through its inspiration, for nearly two thousand years, countless people, rulers and common folk, restrained themselves from doing evil, revealed the good in the depths of their souls and did many good deeds. Some of them rose to the level of righteous and pious ones of the nations of the world, and among them were also heads of churches and simple people who stood up and defended persecuted Jews; there were even pious ones who risked their lives to save Jews. Apparently, the more they connected to the foundations of faith and morality in the Tanakh, to the values of learning explained in the Torah, and to the value of man's responsibility before God, the more inspiration they received for righteousness and good deeds. An example from recent generations is Vladimir Solovyov (5613-5660; 1853-1900), who was a devout Christian theologian, and yet expressed love for the people of Israel and opposed their persecution, to the point that our master Rav Kook crowned him with the title "the pious one among the nations of the world in our day" (Igrot Ha-Re'aya 1:18). Here is the place to mention also one of the greatest of the Righteous Among the Nations, the head of the Church in Bulgaria, Metropolitan Stefan, who stood heroically against the king and the Nazi order to send all the Jews of Bulgaria to be murdered in the death camps. He even declared that anyone who took part in handing over a Jew would be excommunicated by the Church, including the king. All the bishops in Bulgaria acted under his inspiration, and thus most of the Jews of Bulgaria were saved. Likewise, following a decision of the heads of the Protestant Church in France, Christians risked their lives to save Jews.

And behold, the hour has come of which the prophets prophesied. The sound of the weeping of Raḥel our mother has begun to be heard, the lament and bitter weeping of the mother who refused to be comforted for her children who were exiled from their land and were tormented and afflicted in all the exiles. And God answered: "Refrain your voice from weeping and your eyes from tears, for there is reward for your work, says the Lord, and they shall return from the land of the enemy. And there is hope for your future, says the Lord, and the children shall return to their own border" (Yirmiyahu 31:14-16).

Parallel to the appearance of the first rays of light of the redemption of Israel, and to the return of the first Jews to the Land of Israel, God-fearing Christians began to return to the Tanakh, which they call the "Old Testament," and learned from it about God's love for His people Israel and about the redemption awaiting them and the world. Through this they learned to appreciate the self-sacrifice of the Jews, who even throughout the long exile, despite all the suffering, did not stop believing in and loving the Lord, the God of their fathers, and cleaving to His Torah and His mitzvot. The voice of God, who causes salvation to sprout for His people, was heard in their ears. "For thus says the Lord: Sing with gladness for Yaakov, and shout at the head of the nations; proclaim, praise and say: O Lord, save Your people, the remnant of Israel. Behold, I will bring them from the north country and gather them from the uttermost parts of the earth; among them the blind and the lame, the woman with child and her that travails with child together; a great company shall return here. They shall come with weeping, and with supplications will I lead them; I will cause them to walk by rivers of water, in a straight way in which they shall not stumble, for I am a father to Israel, and Efrayim is My firstborn. Hear the word of the Lord, O nations, and declare it in the islands afar off, and say: He who scattered Israel will gather him, and keep him as a shepherd does his flock" (Yirmiyahu 31:6-9). Thus righteous and pious Christians arose, mainly from among the Evangelicals belonging to the Protestant stream, who expressed love for Israel and supported the return of Israel to their land, foremost among them Lord Balfour. As the prophecies were progressively fulfilled, more and more Christians returned to the Tanakh, and through it to love of Israel and to recognition of their right to their land, and they accompany with prayers and deeds the wondrous miracle of the return of Israel to their land.

An important change took place in parallel also within the Catholic stream, which is the largest in the Christian world. Following the Holocaust and the establishment of the State of Israel, the Church made a reckoning of conscience about the attitude of Christians toward Jews, and in a series of important decisions they changed their attitude toward Jews in principle. They removed from the Jews as a whole the charge of "deicide," expressed sorrow that Christians had hated and persecuted Jews, and even recognised that God's choice of Israel has not been annulled, and that the Jewish people is still called God's people, and the way of the Torah and mitzvot is fitting for it. Although these decisions aroused opposition among haters of the Jews, the Church continued to affirm them. This change for the better is so surprising and astonishing that many Jews, who still remember all the suffering and torment, find it hard to believe that it is indeed so, and some are even certain that all these changes are a deception intended to draw Jews to Christianity in a more sophisticated way.3

But to our sorrow, there are still many Christians who continue the legacy of hatred toward Israel. Even among those who love [Israel], many still hope that Israel will accept the Christian faith, even if in practice they do not act toward that end. We pray that hatred, murderousness and idolatry be uprooted, as in the words of the prophet Zekharia (9:7): "And I will take away his blood out of his mouth, and his abominations from between his teeth – and he too shall remain for our God." And the legacy of all those righteous and pious Christians of all generations will be the foundation for advancing the Christian religion on a path of pure and beneficent faith.

notes_en.en: The significant change took place under the leadership of Pope John XXIII (1881-1963), who was one of the distinguished Righteous Among the Nations, and even before that, during the Holocaust, as the papal envoy in Turkey and Greece, saved many Jews. In the five years he served as pope, he initiated the decision Nostra Aetate, which was the foundation for the change in attitude toward Judaism. In the decision, the charge for the death of "that man" was removed from the Jews as a whole, and opposition to hatred of Israel was expressed. After his death, the Rishon Le-Tziyon, Rav Yitzḥak Nissim, published a statement of sorrow over the grave loss to the members of his faith, which because of "his personality, his courage and the aspirations he sought to realise in a generation of anxiety in the face of destructive wars" may also "sadden all lovers of peace and love of humanity in the world." He further wrote "that he rose above pettiness and demonstrated the supremacy of the spirit," and began to make important corrections and to bring about a meaningful turning point in the Church's attitude toward the Jewish people, and "it is regrettable that before he completed his plans for fostering peace and understanding, he passed from the world." After two more popes, Pope John Paul II (1920-2005) was appointed, who at times expressed a certain respect and love for Jews, and expressed sorrow for wrongs that Christians had caused Jews throughout history. After the Holocaust he worked to return to Judaism Jewish children who had been hidden in monasteries, and refused to baptise them into Christianity. In 2015, a statement was published in the name of a Vatican commission that strengthened the Nostra Aetate decision regarding Jews, adding that God's choice of Israel has never been annulled, and expressing opposition to missionary activity among Jews. All Catholics who agree with these decisions are no longer defined as minim, since they are not hostile to Israel and their religion (see above 5, note 13). And although the Catholic Church consistently supports the position of the Arabs against the State of Israel, following the important decisions mentioned, which have been affirmed, this is no longer the grave, principled and piercing hatred of the minim. And the many Evangelicals who cleave to faith and morality and support Israel's returning to their land and keeping their religion are not only not considered minim, but have even risen to the level of the pious ones of the nations of the world.
